questions.prompt: A settings screen grows from 2 options to 6. What does Hick’s Law predict?

options.text: Nothing changes, as long as every option is clearly labeled
Decision time goes up, and the first options added cost the most
Decision time doubles with every option added
People will always pick the first option

questions.explanation: Decision time grows with the logarithm of the number of choices. Going from two to four hurts more than going from ten to twelve.

questions.prompt: A checkout page offers fourteen shipping options. What’s the biggest risk?

options.text: People read every option carefully and pick the best one
The page takes longer to load
People stall, second-guess, or leave without choosing
People always choose the cheapest option

questions.explanation: Too many comparable options make choosing feel hard, so people delay, regret their pick, or choose nothing at all.

questions.prompt: Which of these is extraneous cognitive load: effort spent on the interface instead of the task?

options.text: Hunting for the Save button because it moves on every screen
Working out which insurance plan fits your budget
Understanding the tax rule a form asks about
Reading the order total before you pay

questions.explanation: The others are part of the task itself. A Save button that moves is pure interface cost, and that’s the load we can remove.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many chunks of information can people hold in working memory at once?

options.text: One
About four
About twelve
As many as they need, if they concentrate

questions.explanation: Current research puts it at about four chunks. Don’t make people carry details from one screen to the next.

questions.prompt: A teammate says, “Miller’s Law means menus can’t have more than seven items.” What’s the best response?

options.text: Agreed, seven is a hard limit
The real limit is five
Miller’s Law only applies to phone numbers
“Seven, plus or minus two” is about memory. People scan menus; they don’t memorize them

questions.explanation: Miller’s Law is a warning about memory, not a rule about menus. Use it to justify chunking, not arbitrary item limits.

questions.prompt: Why show a card number as 4242 4242 4242 4242 instead of one unbroken string?

options.text: Small groups are easier to scan, check and remember
It takes up less space
The number won’t work without the spaces
It makes the number harder to copy

questions.explanation: Grouping turns sixteen digits into four chunks, so people can check what they typed.

questions.prompt: People keep missing an important notice that’s styled like a promotional banner. What’s happening?

options.text: The notice is too short
People don’t care about notices
People tune out anything that looks like an ad (banner blindness)
The banner needs an animation

questions.explanation: People focus on what fits their goal and filter out things that look like ads. Important information shouldn’t look like a promotion.
